title: Honda's Cheapest SUV Can't Dethrone It's Best-Selling Sibling - Here's Why - CarBuzz
content: Added a section that talks about the CR-V TrailSport in more detail. Buying a Honda SUV for family needs seems like the obvious choice. They offer good reliability, practicality and comfort at a price that will not break the bank. However, in 2026, that choice may be a little confusing to make. With the HR-V and CR-V, Honda has two different propositions to offer in terms of value and practicality. So, which one makes more sense for you between the subcompact HR-V SUV vs the compact CR-V SUV? We compare their engines, exterior, interior and, finally, their price to find out which one is the better deal for you. All information has been sourced from the manufacturer or test drive experience, where available. All prices listed are MSRP, which does not include any offers or additional fees. Automakers reserve the right to update pricing at their own discretion and without notice. The Honda CR-V is available with two powertrains in the US. While the entry-level non-hybrid 1.5L is sufficient for many budget-conscious buyers, especially in the city, the hybrid system features a 1.06-kWh battery and provides more power while boosting efficiency scores throughout all trims. Both engine options are paired with a CVT gearbox. AWD is available as an option on all trims of the CR-V and CR-V Hybrid. For 2026, the powertrains get a new traction-management system for the AWD models to aid maneuverability in low-speed, low-traction situations. While neither engine option is known for its spirited driving dynamics, they are both quiet and smooth at highway speeds and offer good fuel economy in the city. There is also an option for a fuel cell EV powertrain in the CR-V e:FCEV that offers an EPA-estimated rating of 270 miles, but as that is a completely different model and does not rival the HR-V. Hence, we do not include it in this comparison. "New software tuning allows for a simulated rear differential lock at low speeds, which allows the crossover to muscle through slippery terrain if even one wheel has traction." Many have said that if the Honda HR-V has an Achilles heel, it is its engine and gearbox combination. Technically, the HR-V also has two powertrain options, one of them being hybrid. However, the US market only gets the non-hybrid option as of now. While the numbers do not seem too bad on paper, the HR-V shares its non-hybrid engine with the base Civic sedan and hatchback. This is arguably the biggest difference between the Honda CR-V and HR-V. While the engine remained the same, the surrounding chassis got heavier and larger in the shape of the subcompact SUV. As a result, the engine is adequate at city speeds, but feels strained and loud at highway speeds or while overtaking. The CVT gearbox also does not help with the added noise at constant speeds. AWD is available as an option on all trims for a premium of $1,500, much like its bigger brother, the CR-V. The Honda CR-V is bigger in almost every dimension, which results in a more traditional SUV look with a more upright stance. The HR-V is smaller, and appeals to the rising trends of crossovers and subcompact SUVs. Both cars do a good job of being inoffensive to look at, which is exactly what someone is looking for from a dependable Japanese compact SUV. While the CR-V offers multiple trims to appeal to buyers looking for either a family SUV or maybe even a rugged AWD SUV, the HR-V trims are much simpler and offer the basic, urban-focused needs of the market it serves. All-terrain tires and some tweaked cosmetics don't provide much improvement, but neither do they spoil what's already a competent crossover. The exterior on both SUVs does not massively change with each trim, except for the TrailSport trim on the CR-V Hybrid. The HR-V is smaller and will be easier to maneuver in the city or a parking space. If you live in an urban jungle, the HR-V may be better suited to you. But if you have more space to maneuver, the CR-V's bigger dimensions bode well for its interior space. Not only is the HR-V limited in its number of available trim levels, it lacks the brand's popular TrailSport variant. Buyers have flocked to Honda for its off-road oriented trim that's optional on the CR-V, Pilot, Ridgeline, and Passport models. In the CR-V's case, we can see why buyers would choose this over the HR-V's relatively simple lineup. It comes with the same hybrid powertrain as any other hybrid trim; power outputs are the same, as is its e-CVT and standard all-wheel drive. That said, this trim might sway buyers away from the HR-V for its styling and some extra standard features. It comes with standard all-terrain tires that offer improved grip off the pavement, four drive modes including Normal, Snow, Sport, and Econ, roof rails, dual exhaust, and cloth seats with orange stitching. This variant's tires lend to its slightly worse fuel economy compared to the rest of the hybrid lineup, as it gets an estimated 38/33/35 mpg. However, the rest of its design, drive modes, and tires may pull buyers away from other options. The new Honda cabin layout and simple, unlike some other manufacturers experimenting with a plethora of screens and haptic buttons in 2026. The HR-V takes inspiration from the Civic here as well, with a horizontal dashboard and physical climate controls. The honeycomb grille for the air vents adds some texture to an otherwise uneventful front cabin. So, which is bigger, CR-V or HR-V? The HR-V is noticeably smaller inside when compared to the CR-V, especially behind the front row. Adults will find the rear legroom cramped for long rides, and the trunk space is average against its subcompact SUV rivals. The CR-V received an interior tech upgrade for 2026 that makes the 9-inch touchscreen standard across all trims and brings wireless phone charging and connectivity. The dashboard follows a similar ethos of being uncluttered and as easy to use as the HR-V. The biggest difference you will see is the space behind the front row. While the shoulder room and hip room may not be considerably bigger, there is significantly more legroom. Cargo space also sees an almost 60% increase from the HR-V, to a class-leading 39.3 cu-ft expanding to 76.5 cu-ft with the seats folded. Honda has tweaked the HR-V, but base model shoppers will benefit most. Pricing is usually the most important deciding factor when picking between two cars from the same manufacturer. The entry level CR-V starts at $30,920, with prices rising up to $35,400 for the highest non-hybrid trim. The hybrid powertrains naturally demand more money, and start at $35,650 all the way till the Sport Touring Hybrid is priced at $42,550. While that is significantly more than the HR-V in any trim, the non-hybrid CR-V is pretty close in price. You do get more mileage, efficiency and power from the hybrid system. However, the interior and exterior fundamentals remain the same. There is a reason the CR-V has been a class leader in the compact SUV category, as it offers a trim for almost everybody. The HR-V is the entry-level Honda SUV model starting at $26,600. The top of the line trim starts from $30,450. It is interesting to note that the entry-level CR-V is just $470 more than the flagship HR-V trim. While you miss out on features such as leather upholstery, a moon roof, dual-zone parking climate controls and parking sensors among other quality of life features, you get a bigger SUV with a stronger engine and better economy for not much more money. The entry-level CR-V may seem spartan inside when compared to the HR-V. However, with the 2026 update of new tech features for the CR-V, that gap is closer than ever. Honda CR-V vs HR-V Sales Figures Over The Last 5 Years If we look at the sales figures over the last five years between the CR-V and HR-V, you can clearly see just how popular the former is. While the HR-V appeals to a more price-sensitive market where the sales volumes are naturally lower, the CR-V continues to dominate in the larger segment, especially after its redesign in 2023. CR-V's are also known to hold their values better, with price trends showing great stability for the model. The better option between the two compact SUVs from Honda is the CR-V. While the HR-V is cheaper, it is restricted by its engine and performance, and space for more than two people. It also does not have vastly different trims to appeal to a wider audience, something that the CR-V does so well. The price difference is marginal between the non-hybrid CR-V and HR-V, but is significantly more if you want the hybrid powertrain. The CR-V, in both its powertrain options, is a better family SUV with great interior space and reliability to keep you satisfied for many miles. We want to hear from you. title: World Cup schedule today: How to watch Netherlands v Sweden, TV channels & live stream Saturday 20 June - The Guardian
content: Live blog: the latest news from around the tournament Group F is shaping up to be one of the most competitive at the 2026 World Cup with Japan, the Netherlands and Sweden all talented enough to make a deep run. title: Pine64 Pinevoice – A $50 RISC-V Smart Speaker for Home Assistant based on Bouffalo Lab BL606P MCU - CNX Software
content:
Reviews, tutorials and the latest news about embedded systems, IoT, open-source hardware, SBC's, microcontrollers, processors, and more After over two years in the making, Pine64 has now launched the PineVoice (previously PineVox) smart speaker based on the Bouffalo Lab BL606P RISC-V wireless microcontroller with WiFi, Bluetooth, and Zigbee radio interfaces. The device also features two microphones, a speaker, a USB 2.0 OTG port, volume buttons, a mute button with LED, a start/stop button, and four RGB LEDs. The PineVoice smart speaker is mainly designed to work with Home Assistant. The default firmware supports Wyoming Satellite protocol, which, according to the project itself, is now deprecated, and the ESPHome protocol is now preferred. The documentation includes more technical details with PDF schematics for the main and bottom boards, and software resources with links to various repositories for the SDK and firmware development. However, I can’t find the default firmware’s source code for now since there’s nothing specific to the PineVoice. Pine64 explains that the PineVoice is still in early-stage development and may experience performance issues, notably for wake word detection. It should probably be considered as a smart speaker devkit, rather than a consumer device for your Home Assistant setup. This may change in the future if the firmware improves. With that in mind, if you’d like to go ahead, the PineVoice can be purchased for $49.99 on the Pine64 store. It ships with a USB-A to USB-C cable and a Quick Start Guide. Warranty is valid for 30 days. Does it no have a dedicated DSP for advanced audio processing the voice captured from the microphone so that it can do echo cancellation (AEC) and noise suppression, etc. similar to the XMOS XU316 dedicated audio processor chip used in Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition hardware? Far-field voice capture from across a noisy room is usually bad without some kind of advanced audio processing the voice captured from the microphone so that it can do echo cancellation (AEC) and noise suppression, etc. No external DSP, but I can see an AEC circuit with passive components in the PDF schematics. The BL606P also features a built-in audio codec. As Jean-Luc says, no specific DSP hardware.
But, the whole high-performance C906 core is dedicated for audio processing.
That’s also where local wake word detection is. There is plenty of computing power for any DSP audio processing, but currently there is only wake word detection.
Also, there are some T-Head instructions which should be suitable for DSP. Wonder how this compares to the Home Assistant Voice – larger speaker but weaker audio processing?

title: Scotland v Morocco World Cup ratings: Hendry 8, McTominay 7; Brahim Diaz 8, Saibari 8 - The National
content:
Ismael Saibari scored after 71 seconds - the fastest goal of the 2026 World Cup - to secure Morocco’s 1-0 victory over Scotland.
The Atlas Lions moved to four points in Group C, level with Brazil, who lead on goal difference; Scotland remain third on three.
Scotland failed to register a shot on target, despite a stronger second half and late penalty appeals when Scott McTominay went down under Neil El Aynaoui’s challenge.
Jack Hendry impressed for the Scots with an 8/10 performance, while Brahim Diaz and Saibari both earned 8/10 for influential displays in attack.
"I’m proud of the players, but obviously we’re all devastated and disappointed," Scotland coach Steve Clarke said. Ismael Saibari's goal after only two minutes fired Morocco to a 1-0 win over Scotland in Group C of the 2026 World Cup. The result puts ⁠Morocco level on four points at the top of the ⁠group, although Brazil's 3-0 win over Haiti has them on top on goal difference. Scotland are third on three points thanks to last week's win over Haiti and retain a chance of advancing to the Round of 32 as one of the best third-placed teams. World Cup power rankings: All 48 teams rated after opening round of matches They pushed hard for an equaliser in the second half ⁠but never had a shot on target during the match. Scotland's Scott McTominay went down ​under ⁠a challenge from Neil El Aynaoui ‌in the box during the 80th minute, but no foul was called. In the early going, ​Brahim Diaz delivered a pass down Morocco's right flank to Saibari, who found space between two defenders and entered the final third of the pitch unmarked. Saibari drove in the 18-yard box with the ball and lifted a right-footed shot over the right shoulder of Scotland goalkeeper Angus Gunn. It was the fastest goal in the 2026 World Cup and the second goal in two games at the tournament for Saibari. Scotland coach Steve Clarke: "I thought we picked ourselves up in the first half. Maybe we took 10 minutes to get into the game again [after Morocco's goal] because obviously, when you get a setback, it is really difficult to respond. Weaker teams would have crumbled against that quality of opposition but we dug in, we got ourselves back in the game, and started moving the ball about a little bit better. I'm proud of the players, but obviously we’re all devastated and disappointed that we didn’t get the result we wanted." Yassine Bounou, Morocco goalkeeper: "I think we played a very good game against a strong opponent, with players with a lot of experience. I think we had a lot of patience and we were able to create chances, although they were in a very, very low block. In the last 10 minutes they pushed a little more and, when we had to step back, we did it well." Angus Gunn - 6/10: Scotland got off to a disastrous start, which wasn’t his fault. Top save after 17 minutes to prevent Morocco going two up. Saved well on 51 minutes from a corner. Nathan Patterson - 7/10: Right-back was up against it with El Khannouss and Mazraoui pushing onto him. Improved, like his team, in the second half. Grant Hanley - 7/10: Right of the central defensive two and the Hibernian man got it wrong by stepping out to play offside … only to leave Saibari onside to score. Otherwise played well. Jack Hendry - 8/10: Left of the central defensive pair and did well against a dangerous Moroccan break on 50 minutes, then stood his ground against Diaz. Booked. Andy Robertson - 6/10: Left-back delivered an excellent ball towards McGinn at the end of a first half where Scotland didn’t lay a glove on Morocco. Booked. Ryan Christie - 7/10: Holding midfielder was neat on the ball and shot over on 63 minutes after an encouraging passage of play. Much better in the second half. John McGinn - 7/10: Captain of a nervous team who started poorly, but he came to life at the end of the first half with a smart run towards a Robertson cross. Appealed for a 48th-minute penalty, but it wasn’t given. Great cross on 86 minutes towards McTominay. Lewis Ferguson - 7/10: Excellent free-kick after 41 minutes came during Scotland’s only positive spell at the end of the first half. Did well to take the ball from Hakimi on 55 minutes. Kieran Tierney - 6/10: Two shots saved at the end of a poor first half for Scotland. Scott McTominay - 7/10: A key player for Scotland, yet initially almost anonymous in a deeper role than he plays for Napoli. Tripped by El Khannous before a Morocco attack. More advanced in second half and set up Christie on 63, appealed – with justification – for a penalty on 81 minutes. Then shot into side netting late on. Che Adams - 6/10: A lonely soul as Scotland became only the second team in the World Cup not to have a shot in the first half. Ben Gannon-Doak (on for Tierney on 59') - 7/10: Fouled Hakimi within a minute of his introduction, then got away from Mazraoui to cross on 87 minutes. Lyndon Dykes (on for Adams on 71') - 6/10: Header wide from an 85th-minute corner. Kenny McLean (on for Christie on 71') - 7/10: Brought energy to Scotland's attack. Yassine Bounou - 6/10: Another clean sheet for a team who’ve lost one of their past 50 matches. Tested far more in the second half. Noussair Mazraoui - 7/10: Started at left back and had a solid match. Chadi Riad - 8/10: Left central defender and comfortable as Scotland couldn’t get behind them for the first hour. Issa Diop - 7/10: First player to be booked after 23 minutes, but untroubled. Achraf Hakimi - 7/10: Probably the world’s best right-back, Morocco’s captain found space as he played in an advanced role that made his team a 3-4-3 in formation. Neil El Aynaoui - 7/10: Roma midfielder carried the ball forward and outclassed his Scotland counterparts. Ayyoub Bouaddi - 6/10: Superb defensive midfielder is still only 18 and on the wanted list of many top sides. Azzedine Ounahi - 7/10: Strong attacking midfielder helped Morocco dominate. Shot over after 30 minutes. Brahim Diaz - 8/10: Real Madrid forward was a danger on the right, with impressive movement and combinations with Saibari. Quick footed Ismael Saibari - 8/10: Led the line and put Morocco ahead with the quickest goal of the World Cup so far after just 71 seconds with a top finish. Struck the crossbar on 50 minutes. Bilal El Khannouss - 7/10: Another threat who looked a level above anything Scotland had. Missed a big chance on 35 minutes, hitting a shot over. Ayoube Amaimouni-Echghouyab (on for Brahim Diaz on 84').
